Someday Nintendo is going to have to wake up and realize that making watered down sequels of sequels will only stretch so far before apathy wins. They need some new IPs. I don't really think Nintendo needs IPs, they need to just better utilize their existing IPs. You pointed our FZero and Metroid, two franchises which haven't had a new game in the main series in quite some time. Why is Nintendo just sitting on these franchises? They could make an FZero game for Wii U which is basically just FZero GX HD and people would be so excited to play it. Sometimes I think Nintendo gets it in their head that they need to reinvent the wheel every time they release a new game for a major IP, so they sit on franchises like FZero because they feel like there is nothing new to be done with the series. Nintendo needs to realize that people want to play new entries in their favorite series and they don't really care if those games revolutionize the genre (in fact, I'm pretty sure most people would be more happy if the games just stayed the same).

So we end up getting things like Animal Crossing Party and Triforce Heroes, because Nintendo thinks it's not worth it to release just another Animal Crossing game or just another 3DS Zelda, even though this is exactly what people want. They need to be careful with this strategy of focusing on spin offs and new ways of playing old IPs, because people are going to lose interest in the series. Sure, Triforce Heroes will sell even if it is mediocre compared to a "real" Zelda game, because there are so many fans of the IP. But I really don't think anyone is excited about the new Metroid, even the most diehard Metroid fans. It has been so long since a "true" Metroid game has come out that no one feels loyalty to the IP anymore since it doesn't mean what it used to mean. If Nintendo stopped making main series Zelda games (not that I think this is going to happen) and just released stuff like Triforce Heroes and Hyrule Warriors, people would stop caring about the Zelda series too.

Nintendo doesn't need to come up with new IPs when they have stuff like FZero and Metroid sitting on the backburner just begging to have new games made.

Buying gold is rarely a way to make a significant amount of money. The whole point of gold is its stability. When the market is up, stability is less important, and the value of gold drops somewhat; and when the market is down, investors seek to hold value and gold is one way to do that, so gold rises. But these shifts are relatively small compared to the market, and the smallness of those changes is what gold is all about. Over time, the value of gold generally keeps pace with inflation. Holding gold will never be a way to get rich.

However, anyone who's watched daytime television has seen advertisements hawking gold as the next big wave in investment, predicting massive increases in value. Just who is running these commercials; and if gold is such a great investment, why aren't they buying it themselves instead of buying TV ads to sell gold to you? That should tip you off. The companies running these advertisements are financial services companies. They are in the business of lending money, generally at high interest rates. They frankly don't care what you do with the loan, whether you buy gold with it or a jet ski; what they're after is the interest on your loan. Trust me, they make far more money off your interest than they would if they bought gold instead.

Some companies take it a step farther and stamp the gold into non-negotiable coins, often giving some impressive-sounding name for the coin to give the impression it's a valuable piece of currency, prized by collectors. Be skeptical. The vast majority of these are simply a way for them to sell you the gold at a price higher than its actual value as gold; but to anyone you might sell it to, it's only worth the gold it's made from, so you'll lose money. There are some exceptions. South African Krugerrands and American Eagle coins, for example, are minted by governments as a way to facilitate private ownership of gold and do have a value slightly higher than the bullion itself, but their price fluctuates in line with other gold; so they're really of no greater value than just a plain gold bar, just easier to buy and sell.

Do we really need High Dynamic Range?

I think, at least for me, this article really address the desire for DR: "we want to be able to shoot anything, at any time, the way we want. In other words, won't we will always be wanting what we can't have?"

Is it really just another megapixel race? I'm not so sure yet but definitely something to think about.

I like how this article mentions high contrast and low contrast light - that's definitely food for thought the next time I shoot.

My opinion is that Dynamic Range is useful in certain fast-paced scenarios where you do not have time to bracket your shots, as well as a useful tool for beginners who are experimenting with landscapes - that way they are able to get more keepers, and allow them to play and get acquainted with Highlights/Whites and Shadows/Blacks sliders in Lightroom.

Bracketing and a certain amount of Photoshop work is still the best way to bring out the clearest details in landscape work. But honestly, these can be quite daunting for the budding landscape photographer - I should know, I'm one of them!

Interesting OP, interesting comments too. I have used bracketed and stitched pictures for many of my most memorable shots.

Examples: Montreal downtown at night - Saint-Ulric, Quebec

Then there's the bracketed ones, such as: Mount-Royal Cross, Montreal - Montreal Reflection On Tar Pit

And finally, you can count this as "HDR" of sorts, I shoot everything in RAW, meaning I can usually get whiter-than-white and blacker-than-black, scavenging some pictures shot too quickly (I do mostly shows and events, so I don't always have the luxury to get the perfect setting for my shots)

I believe we are far from true HDR, and I would love to have a camera that could actually take for every single pixel (example numbers) up to 20 photons frequency, force and orientation. At that point, I believe we'd have true HDR (as well as refocusing capabilities). For now, it's bound to primaries and capacity to shoot them with more than what the camera can do, stretching the limits.

I'm also a very big fan of traditional photography, and I have a few films with +- 10 ISO emulsions. These are meant to be shot slooooowly, and will provide a very wide range of contrast, from the blackest blacks, to subdued black tones, to grays, to white shades, to (paler shades - couldn't resist) full white in one picture. It will also accentuate contrast, much like local contrast in HDR softwares. So yes, HDR can become an art form in itself.

I see HDR as a tool. You look at a scenery, and you understand you want more than what you currently have available, and you try to get it through any means possible. It's also a cool thing to achieve.

The first example was shot HDR due to the very high contrast of the lights and windows, and blacks elsewhere. The second one was shot directly towards the sun. Didn't want to have a white blotch, nor want to limit my colours and contrasts elsewhere. The 3rd one was an exercise in style, it was dark enough to second guess my walking (not pitch dark either), but I wanted to have proper definition for the cross. And the 4th one, I wanted to capture the shadow of the ever important Mont Royal, back drop from that dark night (please get the Download version - dA recompression is crap to my picture) So I used HDR on these ones.
